title: Shared responsibility model (security of the cloud vs in the cloud)
hook: AWS secures the physical data centers and hypervisors. You secure what you put in the cloud — operating system patches, firewall rules, and who can call which API.

blocks.text: The shared responsibility model splits security duties between AWS and the customer. AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: hardware, global infrastructure, and managed service foundations. You are responsible for security in the cloud: data classification, Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, network configuration, encryption choices, and guest operating system patching on Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) workloads.

entries.plainDefinition: Physical security, hypervisor, and the managed control planes AWS operates.
entries.example: AWS patches the Nitro hypervisor; you do not.

entries.plainDefinition: Configuration and data you control inside your account.
entries.example: Your S3 bucket policy deciding public versus private access.

entries.plainDefinition: AWS takes more of the stack; you configure fewer layers.
entries.example: Amazon RDS manages the database engine; you set credentials and network access.

blocks.text: Most AWS security interview failures come from blaming AWS for customer misconfigurations — public S3 buckets, overly broad IAM policies, missing encryption. The model shifts as you move up the stack: on EC2 you patch the OS; on Lambda AWS patches the runtime; on S3 you own bucket policies and object encryption settings.

blocks.title: Interview one-liner
blocks.body: AWS secures the cloud; you secure what you configure in it. Responsibility shrinks as services become more managed.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: IaaS (EC2)
items.body: You patch OS, configure Security Groups, manage data encryption.

items.title: PaaS (RDS, Lambda)
items.body: AWS patches runtime/engine; you set network access, IAM, and encryption keys.

items.title: SaaS (WorkMail)
items.body: You configure users and data handling; AWS runs the application stack.

snippet.label: CLI: block public S3 access at account level
snippet.explanation: Your responsibility: prevent accidental public buckets. AWS provides the control; you must enable it.

snippet.label: CloudFormation: S3 bucket with encryption and block public access
snippet.code:
Resources:
  AppBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
              SSEAlgorithm: AES256
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
snippet.explanation: Encryption and public access settings are customer configuration — not automatic defaults you can ignore.

snippet.label: CLI: attach least-privilege IAM policy to a role
snippet.explanation: IAM permissions are always your responsibility. Scope actions and resources narrowly.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Assuming AWS encrypts everything by default without checking. Using root account access keys for automation. Leaving Security Groups open to 0.0.0.0/0 because 'it's in the cloud.'

interviewTakeaways: AWS secures the cloud (hardware, hypervisor, managed foundations); you secure configuration and data in the cloud.
Responsibility decreases as services become more managed — but never reaches zero.
Enable S3 Block Public Access and least-privilege IAM before your first production deploy.
60s: Split is AWS vs customer. EC2 you patch OS; Lambda AWS patches runtime; S3 you own bucket policy and encryption. Most breaches are misconfiguration, not AWS infrastructure failure.
Follow-up: who patches the database engine on RDS versus self-managed on EC2?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'AWS handles security' — that gets you rejected because IAM, network rules, and data classification are always yours.
Strong answer: name the specific layer — OS, network, IAM, encryption — and who owns it for the service in question.
Relying on default S3 ACLs without Block Public Access.
Using AdministratorAccess for application roles instead of task-scoped policies.

jsTsCorrelations.note: On EC2 or Lambda you inject secrets via environment variables or Secrets Manager — AWS does not choose your secret storage pattern. That is security in the cloud.
